title: Decidability of restricted elementary real functions
formal: Is the joint first-order truth problem for \(\mathcal R_0\) and \(\mathcal R_1\) decidable, where \(\mathcal R_0=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\mathrm{rexp},\mathrm{rsin},\mathrm{rcos})\) and \(\mathcal R_1\) additionally includes the unrestricted real exponential \(\exp\)? The three restricted functions agree with exponential, sine and cosine on the closed interval \([0,1]\), and equal zero outside it. Precisely, does one ordinary deterministic Turing machine halt on every pair \((b,\varphi)\), with \(b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\varphi\) a first-order sentence in the corresponding language, and correctly decide whether \(\mathcal R_b\models\varphi\), without any unproved number-theoretic hypothesis or oracle?

source_formulation.text: Similarly, it is an open question whether RRE and RRE exp are decidable, but they are also known to be decidable subject to Schanuel’s conjecture […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 4

why: Real polynomial constraints admit exact decision procedures, while analytic functions can express descriptions needed for continuous-system verification. Determining whether the same kind of unconditional symbolic reasoning is possible for these restricted elementary operations would clarify the computational boundary of that extension. The problem concerns exact truth with arbitrary quantifier alternation, beyond numerical approximations to individual function values.
status_note: The 2020 source poses both questions as open. The checked 2025 algorithmic survey continues to state decidability of the stronger theory conditionally on Schanuel’s conjecture, with an explicit caveat about the underlying unpublished argument. Later bounded searches through 2026-09-15 did not find a resolution of the unconditional joint truth problem. These checks do not independently verify the conditional proof or certify an exhaustive status review.

progress.text: Almagor et al. state the two open decidability questions in Section 2, page 107:4. Their Theorem 3.9 invokes the conditional theory for invariant existence; Section 4 treats semialgebraic error sets separately.
Karimov et al., Section 3.2, review the stronger exponential-plus-restricted-trigonometric theory and still make its decidability conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture over the complex numbers.

Jaoui and Kirby post a preprint on integration in finite terms and exponentially algebraic functions. The checked abstract concerns a different family of decision problems, not unrestricted first-order truth in the present finite languages.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is decidability of real theories with elementary functions used in invariant reasoning.

importance.reason: A substantial decidability frontier beyond real algebraic geometry, with direct relevance to verification of analytic dynamical systems. The finite-language restriction isolates the unresolved effectiveness of exact exponential and bounded trigonometric reasoning without hiding undecidability in arbitrary constants or unrestricted periodicity.

sentences: The problem asks whether exact first-order truth is decidable over the real field with exponential, sine and cosine restricted to the unit interval.
It also includes the source’s extended language with unrestricted exponential, using a tag to make both signatures one decision problem.
Inputs are finite sentences with only fixed primitive constants, while all quantified variables range over the standard real numbers.
Known conditional results use Schanuel’s conjecture, and continuous-system invariant questions provide a computational motivation.
A solution must give an unconditional total decision procedure for the joint truth set or prove that none exists.

definitions: The domain of each structure is the standard real field, and every quantifier ranges over all real numbers. The usual functions are \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), \(\sin(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-1)^j x^{2j+1}/(2j+1)!\), and \(\cos(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(-1)^j x^{2j}/(2j)!\). For \(h\in\{\exp,\sin,\cos\}\), its restricted symbol denotes the total function \(rh(x)=h(x)\) if \(0\le x\le1\), and \(rh(x)=0\) otherwise; endpoints are included and angles are in radians. Unrestricted sine and cosine are absent in both languages. For a concrete finite-string encoding, variables are v[q], where q is the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer without leading zero except for zero itself. Terms are the literal constants 0 and 1, variables, and prefix expressions neg(t), add(t,u), mul(t,u), rexp(t), rsin(t), rcos(t), with exp(t) also permitted when b is 1. Formulas are eq(t,u), lt(t,u), not(p), and(p,q), or(p,q), exists(v[j],p), and forall(v[j],p), with their usual first-order meanings and binding scopes; letters t,u,p,q here denote subexpressions. A sentence has no free variables. The input is the literal tag 0 or 1 followed by a colon and the sentence, using the indicated parentheses, commas and brackets, with no whitespace. Malformed strings, open formulas and use of exp in language 0 must be rejected. Formula length, nesting, variable count and quantifier alternation have no fixed upper bound. Only the constants 0 and 1 are primitive, so the input cannot carry arbitrary real constants or noncomputable information. A decision procedure is a single finite program with ordinary finite-alphabet work tapes, no real-operation oracle, no advice and no randomness; no time or space bound is required beyond termination on every input. Exact equality and strict inequality are interpreted in the real structure, with no perturbation promise. The joint problem is one set of finite strings. Because the first language is a sublanguage of the second with the same interpretations, its decidability is equivalent to decidability of the theory of \(\mathcal R_1\). This equivalence concerns deciding both source theories together; undecidability of the joint problem need not imply undecidability of \(\mathcal R_0\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either that the joint truth set defined above is decidable or that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform Turing procedure and prove unconditional termination and exact correctness for every encoded sentence in both languages. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct procedure exists. Conditional decidability assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a procedure for a restricted quantifier fragment, approximate satisfiability, or a numerical routine unable to decide exact zero does not meet the target. No running-time bound is requested.

context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2020 paper explicitly asks about both the restricted elementary real structure and its extension by unrestricted exponentiation. The card preserves those two signatures as one tagged truth problem. Since the larger signature contains the smaller, an algorithm for the larger one answers both, while a negative answer can leave the smaller theory’s separate status unsettled.

The source cites decidability conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture. The 2025 survey by Karimov and coauthors again describes the exponential-plus-restricted-trigonometric result as conditional, records its attribution to Macintyre and Wilkie, and points to Macintyre’s Theorem 3.1(4). It also states the zero-outside-domain convention used here.

The distinction between a tame description of definable sets and an effective truth procedure is essential. A structural theorem about the real sets definable in a language is not by itself an algorithm deciding every sentence in that language. Likewise, computability of the individual analytic functions does not by itself decide all exact equalities involving them.

For continuous linear systems, Almagor and coauthors use these theories in their conditional invariant-existence theorem for error sets described with elementary functions. They separately prove unconditional results for semialgebraic error sets. That restricted application does not establish unconditional decidability of the complete first-order theory.

Jaoui and Kirby’s October 2025 preprint studies exponential algebraicity of solutions to differential equations, using restricted elementary definability. Its stated decidability consequences concern the specified differential-algebraic problems; its abstract does not announce a decision procedure for the full first-order truth problem here.
